column3: A moment, a little while, used after a verb or in a time phrase: 等一會 "wait a moment", 過一會 "after a while", 一會就好 "it will be done in a moment". 會 is the same character as in 我會說 "I can", here in a different sense. 等一下 "wait a moment" is just as common in Taiwan.
column6: Qǐng děng yīhuì, wǒ mǎshàng lái.
column7: Please wait a moment, I will be right there.

column3: Spring. Alone it is mostly in set phrases and compounds: 春天 is the everyday word, and 春假 "spring break", 春節 "Spring Festival (Lunar New Year)". The top of the character is built from sprouting grass and the sun 日 underneath, which fits the season.
column4: 春去夏来，天气越来越热。
column5: 春去夏來，天氣越來越熱。
column6: Chūn qù xià lái, tiānqì yuèláiyuè rè.
column7: Spring goes and summer comes, and the weather gets hotter and hotter.

column3: Summer. On its own it appears in written phrases and compounds, and the everyday word is 夏天: 夏天很熱 "summer is hot". It is also a Chinese surname. 夏 follows 春 in the usual order of the four seasons 春夏秋冬.
column6: Wǒ bù xǐhuān xià, tài rè le.
column7: I don't like summer; it is too hot.

column3: Autumn. Mostly met in 秋天, and in 中秋節 "Mid-Autumn Festival", when families in Taiwan eat mooncakes and grill outdoors. The left part 禾 is a grain plant and 火 is fire, which matches the time of harvest and burning the fields. The same character is in 鞦韆 "swing".
column6: Qiū lái le, tiānqì liáng le.
column7: Autumn has come and the weather has cooled.

column3: Winter, mostly in 冬天 and in compounds such as 冬至 "winter solstice" (when tangyuan are eaten in Taiwan). The same character also stands for a drum beat, 冬冬, but that is rare.
column6: Dōng lái le, wǒ yào chuān hòu wàitào.
column7: Winter has come; I need to wear a thick coat.

column3: Plan, project, as a noun and a verb: 有計畫 "have a plan", 計畫去日本 "plan to go to Japan". Taiwan writes 計畫 with 畫 (the brush 聿 over a field), where the mainland more often writes 计划. 計 is 言 "speech" with 十 "ten", as in counting out a figure.
column7: What plans do you have for the summer vacation?

column3: The Chinese language, especially as it is written and taught to overseas Chinese and in Southeast Asia: 學華文 "study Chinese", 華文老師. In Taiwan, 華語 is the usual name for Mandarin as a language for foreigners to learn, while in everyday speech people just say 中文; 國語, the official name, sounds formal or old-fashioned. 華 is an old form of the "flower" character.
column7: He is studying Chinese.

column3: Toilet, restroom. 廁所 is the plain word and is fine in a shop or school: 請問廁所在哪裡？ "Where is the restroom?" In more polite speech people say 洗手間 or 化妝室, which is what signs in Taiwan often use. The 广 part of 廁 means a building, and 所 means "place".
column7: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

column3: Window. It is mostly met as 窗戶 or 窗子, but on its own in 開窗 "open the window", 關窗, and 窗外 "outside the window". The 穴 on top is a hole or cave, the same part as in 空. Underneath is a chimney-like opening, so the whole is a hole through which light comes in.
column7: Please close the window.

column3: Air conditioning, literally "cold air". In Taiwan 冷氣 is the usual word, and 開冷氣 "turn on the air conditioning" is how everyone says it. 冷 has the ice mark 冫 on the left, and 氣 is "air, gas, breath", as in 天氣 "weather".
column7: The air conditioning is on in the classroom.

column3: An air conditioner, the machine itself: 冷氣 "cold air" plus 機 "machine", the ending of many appliances (照相機, 洗衣機). A unit is counted with 台: 一台冷氣機. In daily speech many people just say 冷氣 for the machine too.
column7: This air conditioner is very noisy.

column3: To have free time: 你有空嗎？ "Are you free?", 我沒空 "I'm not free". It is often followed by a verb: 有空來玩 "come visit when you have time". Here 空 is read kòng "free time, gap", while 空 as "empty" is kōng.
column7: Are you free tomorrow?

column3: Meal, and the measure word for meals: 三餐 "three meals", 一天吃三餐. Mostly in compounds, 早餐 "breakfast", 午餐 "lunch", 晚餐 "dinner", 餐廳 "restaurant". The bottom part 食 means "eat", and the top is a different, older part.
column7: He eats three meals a day.

column3: To kick, and so "to play" kicking games: 踢足球 "play soccer", 踢球. For other ball games Chinese uses other verbs: 打 for baseball and basketball. The left part 足 "foot" gives the meaning; the right part 易 is for the sound, which now only roughly matches.
column7: He likes to play soccer.

column3: Baseball, a very popular sport in Taiwan. The verb is 打: 打棒球 "play baseball", and 看棒球 "watch baseball". 棒 "stick, club" plus 球 "ball". On its own 棒 also means "great": 你很棒 "you are great", 好棒.
column7: My older brother likes playing baseball.

column3: Bicycle, the usual word in Taiwan, literally a "foot-step vehicle": 腳 foot, 踏 step on, 車 vehicle. You ride it with 騎: 騎腳踏車. 自行車 is the written or formal term, and the mainland says it all the time. 踏 has 足 "foot" as its meaning part, and 腳 has ⺼ "flesh, body".
column7: He rides a bicycle to school every day.

column3: Network, the Internet. Taiwan says 網路 where the mainland says 网络. 上網 means "go online", and 網路很慢 "the Internet is slow". 網 is a net, with 糸 "thread" at the left, and 路 is a road, so it is a net of roads.
column7: The Internet here is fast.

column3: To chat. It is a verb plus its object, so it splits: 聊天 "chat", 聊了一個小時的天 "chatted for an hour", and the person is introduced with 跟: 跟朋友聊天. The 聊 is made from 耳 "ear" and a sound part, and 天 is "sky" or "day".
column7: We are chatting in the café.

column3: To chat, the same word as 聊天 with the 兒 ending of northern speech. Taiwan Mandarin uses that ending much less, so in Taiwan you will mostly say and write 聊天. It is a verb with its object and can be split: 聊聊天兒 "have a chat".
column7: Let's sit down and have a chat.

column3: Hello, as said when answering or making a phone call: 喂，你好 or 喂，請問哪位？ It is also a word to call out to someone, but said to a stranger face to face it sounds rude. 口 "mouth" is the meaning part, since it is a spoken sound.
column7: Hello, who are you looking for?

column3: Airport, in full "airplane field": 飛機 plus 場 "field, ground". Most people shorten it to 機場: 去機場 "go to the airport", 機場捷運 "airport MRT line". 場 is used for any large open place (操場, 停車場). 飛 is a picture of a bird flying up.
column7: We take the MRT to the airport.

column3: Crossroads, intersection: 十字 "cross shape" + 路口 "road mouth". Used for giving directions: 在十字路口左轉 "turn left at the intersection", 過了十字路口 "after the intersection". 路口 alone is also common, and 紅綠燈 "traffic light" is usually found there.
column4: 在前面的十字路口左转。
column5: 在前面的十字路口左轉。
column7: Turn left at the intersection ahead.

column3: A bag, usually a soft one of plastic, paper or cloth: 塑膠袋 "plastic bag", 紙袋 "paper bag", 袋子 for any such bag. The measure word is 個 or 個袋子. The ending 子 is neutral. 袋 has 衣 "clothing" below, since a bag, like a pocket 口袋, is made of cloth.
column6: Qǐng gěi wǒ yī ge dàizi.
column7: Please give me a bag.

column3: Camera. 照相 means "take a photo" (照 "shine, take a picture of", 相 "appearance"), and 機 is "machine". 相機 is the shorter everyday form. Counted with 台: 一台照相機. Phone photos are described with 拍照, not 照相機.
column6: Tā yǒu yī tái jiù de zhàoxiàngjī.
column7: He has an old camera.

column3: Hair, only in compounds such as 頭髮 "hair on the head". Written 髮 in Taiwan, because the simplified 发 stands for two characters, 髮 "hair" and 發 "send, develop". The word list gives Taiwan's reading as fǎ (third tone) for it. The 髟 at the top is long hair, and so it appears in other hair words.
column7: Her hair is very long.

column3: Finger, from 手 "hand", 指 "point" and the suffix 頭. 手指 is the shorter, more common form, and 頭 has a neutral tone here. A single finger is counted with 根: 一根手指頭. 指 is made of 扌 "hand" and 旨, which gives the sound.
column7: His finger is injured.

column3: Finger, or toe: 手指頭 for a finger, 腳指頭 for a toe. The suffix 頭 is neutral and means nothing separate. The verb 指 "point" is the same character: 用手指 "point with the hand". A finger is counted with 根.
column7: Don't point your finger at people.

column3: Belly, nearly always as 肚子, with a neutral 子: 肚子餓 "hungry", 肚子痛 "have a stomachache", 拉肚子 "have diarrhea". The ⺼ on the left is "flesh" and the 土 on the right is the sound. 肚子 covers the whole belly, not just the stomach 胃.
column7: I am hungry.

column3: Supermarket: 超級 "super" + 市場 "market". The longer name is fine in writing and on signs; in speech 超市 is shorter and more common. Chains such as 全聯 are simply called 超市. 超 has 走 "run" on the left, meaning to go beyond.
column6: Wǒ cháng qù chāojíshìchǎng mǎi cài.
column7: I often go to the supermarket to buy groceries.

column3: Socks, in compounds such as 襪子. A pair is 一雙襪子. The 衤 on the left is the clothing part, as in 褲 and 裙, and the right part 蔑 is for the sound.
column7: My socks are wet.

column3: Skirt, almost always as 裙子: 穿裙子 "wear a skirt", 短裙 "short skirt". 衤 on the left is the clothing part and 君 on the right gives the sound, which still matches closely (jūn and qún). It is the same left side as in 褲 and 襪, so those three are easy to learn together.
column7: She is wearing a red skirt.

column3: Trousers, pants, usually as 褲子, counted with 條: 一條褲子. Some common kinds are 牛仔褲 "jeans" and 短褲 "shorts". The right half 庫 is the sound and matches exactly (kù), while 衤 on the left says "clothing".
column6: Zhè tiáo kùzi tài cháng le.
column7: These trousers are too long.

column3: Hat, cap, as 帽子, counted with 頂: 一頂帽子. The verb for putting it on is 戴: 戴帽子. The right half 冒 is the sound (both mào), and the 巾 on the left is a piece of cloth.
column7: He is wearing a hat.

column3: Other, before a noun or with 的: 其它的東西 "the other things". Taiwan more often writes the same word as 其他 (with 他), and 其它 is a common variant that is not wrong. 其 is "that" and 它 is "it", so it is "the rest of those".
column6: Qítā de dōngxi wǒ dōu bù yào.
column7: I don't want any of the other things.

column3: Sandwich, a loanword that imitates the English sound: the three characters mean nothing together. Counted with 個 or 份: 一個三明治. Fillings come before it, as in 火腿三明治 "ham sandwich".
column4: 我早上吃了一个三明治。
column5: 我早上吃了一個三明治。
column6: Wǒ zǎoshang chī le yī ge sānmíngzhì.
column7: I ate a sandwich this morning.

column3: Hamburger, from the name of the German city Hamburg: 漢 (the Han people) and 堡 ("fortress") are used here only for their sound. Taiwan says 漢堡, and the mainland 漢堡包. A burger place is a 漢堡店. The earth part 土 at the bottom of 堡 is for walls and forts.
column7: I want to eat a hamburger at noon.

column3: Snacks, pastries, dessert, things eaten between meals or after: 吃點心 "have a snack". The characters mean "touch the heart". 點心 is also the Cantonese "dim sum" that you eat at yum cha; in Taiwan the word more often means small sweets and cakes. 心 is neutral in speech.
column4: 下午我们吃了一些点心。
column5: 下午我們吃了一些點心。
column6: Xiàwǔ wǒmen chī le yīxiē diǎnxin.
column7: We ate some snacks this afternoon.

column3: Ice cream. 冰 is "ice", and 淇淋 imitates the English "cream" in sound, with water marks 氵 on both characters, since it is a cold, soft food. Counted with 球 for scoops and 支 for a cone: 一球冰淇淋.
column7: I often eat ice cream in summer.

column3: Green vegetables, leafy greens in particular. In Taiwan 青菜 is also what people mean by "vegetables" on a menu, as in 炒青菜 "stir-fried greens" or 燙青菜. It is what children are told to eat: 要多吃青菜. 青 is "green or blue-green" and 菜 means both "vegetable" and "dish".
column7: Children should eat more green vegetables.

column3: Knife, a general word: 一把刀子. For a dining table knife you can say 餐刀, and for a fruit knife 水果刀. 刀 is a picture of a blade, and is the form 刂 in words like 刺 or 別 at the right of a character.
column6: Qǐng gěi wǒ yī bǎ dāozi.
column7: Please give me a knife.

column3: Spoon, a soup spoon or a large spoon: 湯 "soup" + 匙 "spoon". In Taiwan 湯匙 is the everyday word for any spoon, counted with 支: 一支湯匙. The 匙 here is read chí, and the same character is read shi in 鑰匙 "key". 匕 on its left is the old picture of a spoon.
column6: Qǐng gěi wǒ yī zhī tāngchí.
column7: Please give me a spoon.

column3: To bake, roast, grill: 烤麵包 "toast bread", 烤雞 "roast chicken", 烤肉 "barbecue" (which Taiwanese families do outdoors at the Mid-Autumn Festival). It can also mean "warm oneself by a fire". 火 is the meaning part, and 考 the sound, which matches exactly.
column6: Wǒ xiǎng kǎo yī ge dàngāo.
column7: I want to bake a cake.

column3: A spoken particle at the end of a sentence, a blend of 了 and 啊: it shows that something is news or is said with feeling. 我到啦！ "I'm here!", 好啦 "okay, okay", 來啦 "I'm coming". It is friendly and informal, so keep it out of formal writing. It can also follow items in a list, as in 蘋果啦、香蕉啦 "apples, bananas and so on".
column7: I'm here!

column3: Put after a verb, it means "a little, for a moment" and makes a request softer or lighter: 看一下 "take a look", 等一下 "wait a moment", 幫我一下 "give me a hand". It can also mean "suddenly": 一下子 is more usual for that. 下 is a short stroke under a long one, as the opposite of 上.
column7: Please take a look.
